newsitem.title: CHINA: China's economic frontline scene of HK takeover.
newsitem.headline: China's economic frontline scene of HK takeover.

text.p: The border city of Shenzhen, for 18 years a staging post for China's economic reforms, becomes a another frontline this week when the People's Liberation Army crosses to claim Hong Kong for the motherland.
China will mark the end of what it calls more than 150 years of national humiliation when 4,000 troops leave this once-sleepy swamp by air, sea and land to take back the British colony.
Shenzhen is festooned with red lanterns and banners welcoming the return of Hong Kong, seized by the victorious British in Opium Wars against the Qing Dynasty.
The skies will explode on Monday in a display of 1,997 different fireworks, starting at 11.30 p.m. (1530 GMT) and counting down the minutes to the midnight handover of sovereignty.
Officials may fear some people will try to cross into Hong Kong at midnight, believing a popular myth that the sovereignty shift opens a tightly-controlled border to booming Hong Kong.
However, late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping recovered Hong Kong under a "one country, two systems" that leaves it autonomous and border crossings unchanged.
But for most Chinese, Shenzhen itself is enough of a lure to fulfil Deng's "get rich" goal.
It was in Shenzhen that Deng launched his dream for China's future as an economic heavyweight, in 1979 declaring it the country's first Special Economic Zone.
More than three million people have since flocked to seek their fortune, transforming the once sleepy hollow into a sprawling city of glass and concrete towers.
Deng's face gleams benignly over the city from a giant billboard that competes for attention with an electronic tickertape detailing local stock prices.
Between 1979 and the end of 1996, Shenzhen's special status attracted $7.63 billion of investment from Hong Kong alone. That accounts for about 70 percent of total foreign investment.
Hong Kong money has poured into hotels, property, textiles, garments, electronics, toys and watches.

This helped to power Shenzhen's industrial growth to 25 percent in 1995. Per capita gross domestic product that year was 20,000 yuan, compared with Shanghai, China's economic heartland, where the figure is expected to reach 25,000 yuan this year.

One price of this explosive growth has been a reputation as a Wild West vice pit. The city has earned itself the nickname "Second Wife Village" as growing numbers of Hong Kong men buy cheap flats and install local mistresses.
Kidnappings occur and prostitution seems widespread.
This anything-goes attitude has fuelled Shenzhen's stock market -- the scene in 1992 of fatal riots when a million people queued for lottery tickets giving them the right to buy shares,
The market is one of two in China -- the other is in Shanghai -- that together recently matched the daily turnover of Hong Kong's exchange, on Friday of about $3 billion.
The benefits for Shenzhen in Hong Kong's handover include the consolidation of their economic links, analysts said.
Hong Kong has provided Shenzhen with a model, said one Chinese reporter.

"Right now Shenzhen is less well regulated, but that just reflects the immaturity of China's economy as a whole," he said. "Over time, Shenzhen will become more and more like Hong Kong, more market-driven."
